extracted.intended_audience: conference reviewers (ICLR 2025) and researchers building LLM-assisted peer-review tools / area chairs
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and evaluation rubrics for writing and (LLM-assisted) assessing conference peer reviews, including per-dimension rating scales, actionable question guidance, an automated report-card schema, and LLM-judge evaluation procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Summary
rubrics_metrics.description: Briefly summarize the paper and its contributions. This is not the place to critique the paper; the authors should generally agree with a well-written summary. Do not paste the abstract; provide the summary in your own understanding after reading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide a concise, neutral summary of contributions in your own words (not a copy of the abstract). Keep critique for other sections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strengths and Weaknesses
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide a thorough assessment of the strengths and weaknesses of the paper; a useful mental framing is to think of reasons you might accept or reject the paper. Touch on the key dimensions (quality, clarity, significance, originality).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: List concrete reasons to accept or reject. Relate strengths/weaknesses to other rating entries. Be thorough and balanced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality (technical soundness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the submission technically sound? Are claims well supported (e.g., by theoretical analysis or experimental results)? Are the methods used appropriate? Is this a complete piece of work or work in progress? Are the authors careful and honest about evaluating both strengths and weaknesses?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assign a numeric rating: 4=excellent, 3=good, 2=fair, 1=poor. Use evidence from the paper (theorems, experiments, analyses) to justify the rating. Consider reproducibility and rigor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the submission clearly written and well organized? Does it adequately inform the reader? A superbly written paper provides enough information for an expert reader to reproduce results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assign a numeric rating: 4=excellent, 3=good, 2=fair, 1=poor. If unclear, provide specific suggestions for improving organization, exposition, and what to add to enable reproduction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Significance
rubrics_metrics.description: Are the results impactful for the community? Are other researchers or practitioners likely to use the ideas or build on them? Does the submission address a difficult task better than previous work or advance understanding in a demonstrable way?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assign a numeric rating: 4=excellent, 3=good, 2=fair, 1=poor. Consider novelty of conclusions, utility of the method, and prospective adoption by the field.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the work provide new insights, deepen understanding, or highlight important properties of existing methods? Is it clear how this work differs from previous contributions, with relevant citations provided? Does it introduce novel tasks or methods, or a novel combination of existing techniques with well-articulated reasoning?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assign a numeric rating: 4=excellent, 3=good, 2=fair, 1=poor. Note: originality need not be an entirely new method — new insights or thorough evaluations can be original.

rubrics_metrics.name: Questions (actionable suggestions)
rubrics_metrics.description: List and carefully describe questions and suggestions for the authors focusing on key points, ideally around 3–5, that are actionable with clear guidance. Think of things where a response can change your opinion, clarify confusion, or address a limitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide explicit, prioritized, and actionable items. You are strongly encouraged to state the clear criteria under which your evaluation score could increase or decrease to make the rebuttal phase productive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations and Societal Impact
rubrics_metrics.description: Have the authors adequately addressed limitations and potential negative societal impact of their work? If so, indicate 'yes'; otherwise include constructive suggestions for improvement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reward transparency: authors should be rewarded rather than punished for being upfront about limitations. Provide concrete mitigation suggestions where relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overall score (10-point scale)
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide an overall score for the submission using the 10→1 choices: 10 Strong Accept; 9 Accept; 8 Weak Accept; 7 Borderline Accept; 6 Weak Reject; 5 Reject; 4 Strong Reject; 3 Serious Reject; 2 Severe Reject; 1 Desk Reject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each numeric choice has a descriptive definition (e.g., '10: Technically flawless with groundbreaking impact; 1: Not suitable for review due to major violations or out of scope'). Use the prior per-dimension assessments to justify the overall score.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidence score (1–5)
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide a confidence score indicating how confident you are in your evaluation: 5=absolutely certain (very familiar and checked details); 4=confident; 3=fairly confident; 2=willing to defend but likely not fully understanding central parts; 1=educated guess (not in area).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain sources of uncertainty when confidence is low (e.g., unfamiliarity with related work or math details not checked).

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not equate 'no' answers with rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: Remember that answering 'no' to some questions is typically not grounds for rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use judgment across multiple dimensions; isolated 'no' responses should be contextualized rather than used as automatic rejection triggers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formatting: allow Markdown/LaTeX in review
rubrics_metrics.description: You can incorporate Markdown and LaTeX into your review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use formulas and formatted text where it helps clarity (e.g., to reproduce or point to equations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Automated Report Card: Coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: Coverage: Does the review touch novelty, significance, technical soundness, and presentation? (Example system output noted that omitting empirical validation, related-work depth, or ethical considerations is a shortcoming.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Score 1–5 (Scale: 1 Poor – 5 Excellent). In automated report cards, Coverage had weight 0.30. Explicitly note if key dimensions (empirical validation, ethics, related work) are missing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Automated Report Card: Specificity
rubrics_metrics.description: Specificity: Does the review pinpoint concrete issues (examples, clearer exposition) and provide page/line references and concrete rewrites rather than high-level questions?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Score 1–5. In the example, Specificity had weight 0.25. Prefer surgically actionable feedback (line-level edits, figure suggestions, exemplar mini-case studies).

rubrics_metrics.name: Automated Report Card: Evidence Base
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence Base: Does the review substantiate claims with citations, quotations, equations, or empirical numbers rather than vague assertions?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Score 1–5. In the example, Evidence Base had weight 0.20. Ask for specific quotes/paraphrases or numerical evidence when critiquing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Automated Report Card: Constructiveness & Tone
rubrics_metrics.description: Constructiveness & Tone: Is the review polite, professional, and encouraging, suggesting revisions rather than dismissing authors?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Score 1–5. In the example, this dimension had weight 0.25. Detect and flag unprofessional or non-constructive phrasing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Automated Report Card: Weighted Composite
rubrics_metrics.description: Compute a weighted composite review-quality score using the per-dimension scores and their weights (example weights: Coverage 0.30, Specificity 0.25, Evidence 0.20, Constructiveness 0.25).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report composite on same scale (e.g., 1–5). Use composite to standardize feedback quality signals for area chairs and to nudge reviewers toward evidence-based critiques.

rubrics_metrics.name: LLM-as-Judge semantic-coverage protocol
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a 'generated' and a 'real' textual statement, create a checklist of distinct points in the real statement, then count how many generated points overlap with that checklist and return counts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Return format: 'Real points: <number> - [<point1>, <point2>, …]  Hits (overlap): <number>'. Use the judge to determine per-human-point whether AI captured it; compute precision (AI points that are valid) and recall (human points captured by AI).

rubrics_metrics.name: Review-component generation via Few-Shot ICL prompts
rubrics_metrics.description: Prompt structure for generating potential strengths/weaknesses: include REVIEW_GUIDELINES, a few example papers (title, abstract, content, human review, strengths/weaknesses, initial score), then the test paper info and ask the LLM to infer key strengths and weaknesses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use concrete examples in the prompt (few-shot), include real human review excerpts as demonstrations. Provide explicit fields (POTENTIAL_STRENGTHS, POTENTIAL_WEAKNESSES, INITIAL_SCORE, INITIAL_REVIEW, AUTHOR_REBUTTAL) to guide generation. This is a production guideline for LLM-assisted review generation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rating-prediction task guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Given paper content, initial review, initial score, and author rebuttal, predict the final score after rebuttal. Return only a single number (final rating).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Predicting exact final scores is hard; it may be more informative to predict direction of change (increase/decrease/no change) and magnitude (e.g., +/-1). This task requires data where reviewers explicitly state why their score changed (or not).

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation notes: LLM-as-judge metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: When using an LLM judge for semantic coverage, calculate precision and recall by comparing AI-generated points to human review points and use these as evaluation metrics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a recommended evaluation protocol: produce human-point checklist, label overlaps, compute precision = (#AI points that are valid) / (#AI points), recall = (#human points captured) / (#human points). Use both to assess coverage and faithfulness.
